units.source_excerpt: In our paper, we construct a mathematical model for estimating total leaf mass of a tree and investigating the relationship between leaf shape and tree profile.
units.function: State the two requested analytical outputs.

features.clause_structure: one model plus two parallel gerunds

units.reusable_pattern: We construct {model} to estimate {quantity_1} and investigate {relationship_2}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not merge two targets unless both receive distinct methods and results.

units.source_excerpt: Our approach consists of two main models.
units.function: Announce the model architecture before details.
units.reusable_pattern: The approach combines {count} models: {model_1} for {role_1} and {model_2} for {role_2}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not announce multiple models without explaining their dependency or division of labor.
Do not describe complementary models as baseline and extension.

units.source_excerpt: The vector tree model uses vector and linear transformation to simulate the geometrical structures of a tree, based on empirical and theoretical research on tree structures. A key assumption for this model is that the branching structure of a tree is paracladial.
units.function: Define the first model, representation, evidence basis, and key assumption.
units.reusable_pattern: The {model} uses {formalism} to represent {output}; its key assumption is {assumption}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call empirical and theoretical research a calibration without naming sources and parameters.

units.source_excerpt: The sunlight model simulates light irradiance inside the tree crown. It starts by simulating the spiral motion of the sun in the course of a year using the brightness function for the sky. Then, the sunlight irradiance inside the tree crown is evaluated using a model based on the Monsi-Saeki equation.
units.function: Explain the second model as an ordered sky-to-crown computation.
units.reusable_pattern: The {model} first computes {upstream_state} using {method_1}, then passes it to {method_2} to obtain {downstream_output}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use starts and then if the downstream model does not consume the upstream output.
This within-model handoff is not evidence of a baseline-to-extension model staircase.

units.source_excerpt: We use the vector tree model to generate different tree profiles. We change the leaf shape under the same branching structure and see whether the real world leaf shape maximizes sunlight exposure among different shapes.
units.function: Define a controlled comparison for leaf shape.
units.reusable_pattern: Holding {structure} fixed, we vary {factor} across {alternatives} and test whether {observed_design} maximizes {metric}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call a comparison controlled if other geometry or parameters change.
Do not infer a global optimum from a small candidate set.

units.source_excerpt: Projection of shadow is used to measure sunlight exposure. Spherical integration is used to calculate the weighted sunlight exposure rate based on the brightness function for the sky.
units.function: Operationalize the comparison metric and its aggregation.
units.reusable_pattern: We measure {construct} by {local_proxy} and aggregate it over {domain} using {weighting_function}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat projected shadow as exposure without checking occlusion, direction, and normalization.

units.source_excerpt: For each tree branching structure, leaves of three different leaf shapes are tested for the total amount of exposure to the sunlight. Comparing the simulated data to real-life data, we found that leaf shapes generally maximize the total exposure.
units.function: Report candidate-set size, external comparison, and the main shape finding.

features.clause_structure: test sentence plus participial comparison sentence

units.reusable_pattern: For each {structure}, we test {count} {alternatives}; compared with {external_data}, the observed design {bounded_result}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not say generally maximizes when only three shapes are tested.
Real-life data must name the dataset and match criterion.

units.source_excerpt: Furthermore, our algorithm is good for medium and small sized leafs, but tends to be unreliable and generate answers with large variance for large sized leaves.
units.function: Carry a size-dependent failure boundary onto the summary page.

prohibited_generalizations: Replace good and unreliable with an error, variance, or coverage threshold.
Use leaves, not leafs.

units.source_excerpt: To estimate the total leaf mass of a tree, we incorporate the tree profile with the photosynthesis model, and use indexes like leaf mass per area (LMA) and leaf area index (LAI) to estimate the total leaf mass of a tree.
units.function: Map the second deliverable to its model combination and indices.

prohibited_generalizations: Do not repeat estimate without explaining how the indices combine.

units.source_excerpt: Photosynthesis rates are assumed to be affected only by sunlight irradiance.

prohibited_generalizations: Do not state only as a universal biological fact; label the model scope and test omitted drivers.

units.source_excerpt: We compute the leaf mass of Cinnamomum camphora using this proposed method.

prohibited_generalizations: Do not generalize beyond the case without cross-species validation.

units.source_excerpt: Comparing to the real-life data, our method is accurate enough with the limited amount of data.

units.source_excerpt: In this paper we present a mathematical model for investigating the relationship between tree profiles and leaf shapes and estimating the total leaf mass of a tree. Specifically, we created a tree profile using 3-dimensional coordinates and linear transformation. We simulate the sunlight irradiance in the tree crown using the brightness function of the sky and Monsi and Saeki equation.
units.function: State the two targets and introduce the two foundational models.

features.clause_structure: purpose sentence plus two method sentences

units.reusable_pattern: We address {targets} by constructing {state_1} with {method_1}, then estimating {state_2} with {method_2}.
prohibited_generalizations: Keep method tense consistent and distinguish work performed from paper organization.

units.source_excerpt: We then incorporate the sunlight irradiance into different tree profiles to find a leaf shape that maximizes sunlight exposure. The chosen shapes match with real leaf shapes, suggesting a close relationship between leaf shape and tree profile.
units.function: Preview the first application, result, and interpretation.

features.voice: active first-person plural then result subject

units.reusable_pattern: Passing {upstream_output} into {application_model}, we select {design}; agreement with {observed_design} supports {bounded_interpretation}.
prohibited_generalizations: A match among a limited candidate set does not prove that the real shape globally maximizes exposure.
Suggestion language does not repair missing error metrics.

units.source_excerpt: We then incorporate the tree profile with the photosynthesis model (Tsukaya, 2006), and use indexes like leaf mass per area (LMA) and leaf area index (LAI) to estimate the total leaf mass of a tree.
units.function: Preview the second application and its dependent indices.
units.reusable_pattern: We pass {profile_output} to {process_model}, derive {index_1} and {index_2}, and estimate {final_quantity}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use indexes like when the exact indices are essential; name and define them.

units.source_excerpt: Our objective is to create a spatial structure of the tree crown (branching structure and leaf distribution). We use vectors to simulate leaf shape, distribution of leaves on branches, and the tree profile/branching structure. Linear transformation of vectors is used to simulate the relationship between daughter branch and parent branch.
units.function: Define the first foundation model from objective through representation to relational mechanism.
units.reusable_pattern: The {model} constructs {state}; it represents {components} with {formalism} and links {relation} through {transformation}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not list representations without stating the generated state consumed downstream.

units.source_excerpt: Our objective is to simulate solar irradiance across a year. Brightness function over the celestial sphere is used to describe solar irradiance from different directions, Monsi and Saeki equation is used to calculate the light attenuation in a tree crown due to overlapping of leaf shadows.
units.function: Define the second foundation model and its two-stage irradiance calculation.

features.clause_structure: objective sentence plus comma splice of two methods

units.reusable_pattern: The {model} estimates {target}; {method_1} provides {boundary_input}, and {method_2} propagates it through {system}.
prohibited_generalizations: Avoid comma splices; separate sequential model stages.
Do not misclassify two complementary models as a baseline and extension.

units.source_excerpt: We use the vector tree model to construct different tree profiles. Combining the tree profile with the sunlight model, we are able to calculate the sunlight exposure rate of the leaves. We then adopt different leaf shapes for the same tree profile and find the one that maximizes the sunlight exposure.
units.function: Show how the two foundation models combine in the first application.
units.reusable_pattern: We use {model_1} to create {state}, combine it with {model_2} to compute {metric}, then hold {state} fixed while varying {design}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call this causal unless the comparison controls all other relevant variables.

units.source_excerpt: Comparing this chosen leaf shape with the real leaf shape of the tree, if there is a match, we may conclude that the leaf shape is associated with the tree profile in that it maximizes the sunlight exposure.
units.function: State the inference rule from simulated optimum to observed morphology.
units.reusable_pattern: If {predicted_design} matches {observed_design} within {tolerance}, this supports {bounded_association}, subject to {alternative_explanations}.
prohibited_generalizations: A shape match does not establish that exposure caused the real shape.
Define the match metric and candidate-space coverage.

units.source_excerpt: Given a tree, we use the vector tree model to simulate its profile, and use the sunlight model to determine the light irradiance at each leaf. Then, we derive the relationship between light irradiance and the leaf mass per area (LMA) according to a photosynthesis model. Thus, we can derive the LMA for each leaf and calculate the weighted average LMA for the entire tree.
units.function: Trace profile and irradiance outputs into leaf-level and tree-level LMA.
units.reusable_pattern: Given {input}, {model_1} yields {state_1}; {model_2} yields {state_2}; {process_model} maps these to {local_output}, which is aggregated as {system_output}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not omit weighting definitions or assume every leaf follows the same irradiance-to-LMA relation.

units.source_excerpt: We then use the sunlight model again to find the shadow of the tree crown and calculate the total leaf area of the tree using leaf area index (LAI). Finally, the total leaf mass is calculated by multiplying LMA with the total leaf area.
units.function: Complete the dependency chain from crown shadow to leaf area and total mass.
units.reusable_pattern: Using {model} again, we derive {area_or_state} via {index}; finally, {final_output}={component_1} times {component_2}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not hide unit compatibility or whether LMA is weighted consistently with total area.

units.source_excerpt: Photosynthesis rate is assumed to be affected only by the rate of light irradiance. Other factors such as CO2 concentration in the air are assumed to be homogeneous at any part of the tree crown.
units.function: State a retained driver and neutralize an omitted spatial factor.
units.reusable_pattern: We retain {driver} as the spatially varying input and treat {omitted_factor} as homogeneous within {domain}.
prohibited_generalizations: Homogeneity must be tested or bounded; it is not equivalent to no effect.

units.source_excerpt: We raise a hypothesis that for any tree profile, the leaf shape will maximize its exposure to sunlight. To test this hypothesis, we calculate the sunlight exposure rate for each type of leaf shape under a given branching structure.
units.function: Pair a mechanism hypothesis with its controlled test metric.

prohibited_generalizations: Do not declare the hypothesis true from one matched shape without tolerance, alternatives, and uncertainty.

units.section: 4.2 Matching leaf shape with tree profile
units.source_excerpt: Since the results are generally expected, our hypothesis stands, i.e. there is correlation between leaf shapes and tree structures: leaf shapes tend to maximize sunlight exposure of this tree. This proves insights into why leaves have different shapes. A larger pool of tree profiles should be studied using this model before we can draw a solid conclusion on the exact relationship.

prohibited_generalizations: Generally expected is not a validation metric.

units.source_excerpt: This algorithm works satisfactorily for small leaf size. However, as we have seen in the Japanese banana tree example, when leaf size is big, this algorithm tends to generate similar results for different leaf shapes. Thus, we may improve our algorithm to calculate leaf shadows for big size leafs.

units.section: 8 Letter to a scientific journal editor
units.source_excerpt: We introduce the concept of Sunlight Exposure Rate (SE) as a metric studying the level of exposure of leaves to sunlight. Given a type of leaf shape, strong correlation exists between total leaf area and total ground shade area. The quotient, which is defined as SE can be used to evaluate the relationship between leaf shape, leaf distribution, and sunlight.
units.function: Translate a model contribution into a named metric and intended use.
units.reusable_pattern: We define {metric} as {numerator}/{denominator} to measure {construct}; it is used to compare {alternatives} within {scope}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim strong correlation without a coefficient, sample, and uncertainty.
Keep stakeholder prose consistent with the implemented area calculation.

units.source_excerpt: We first introduce two models which will be useful in the latter applications:

units.source_excerpt: Trees are assumed to be paracladial, i.e. if any branch is cut off, it has the same structural characteristics, apart from size, as the parent from which it is cut.

units.source_excerpt: To classify a given leaf to one of the four basic shape categories, we focus on 3 factors of the leaf: shape convexity, leaf index (ratio of leaf length to leaf width), and the position of the longest width on a leaf.

units.source_excerpt: In our model, for each branch, we grow the leaves on branch p according to the archived Basic phyllotaxis patterns for different species. The spacing between two different potential leaf spots is decided by function d(I). At each potential spot, the leaf appears with probability p(I).

units.source_excerpt: By modeling the sun radiation using brightness function, and using Monsi-Saeki equation to describe the light attenuation within a tree crown, we will be able to calculate light irradiance at any point within the tree crown.

units.source_excerpt: Thus, since we know the orbit of the sun in the course of a year, the brightness function can be derived by integration of Ea over time (t). This should be done by computer simulation and discretization of the spiral trajectory is used for ease of implementation.
